questions.stem: Liam, 10, has moderate intellectual disability and uses only a few single words. He has settled with his tablet after you greeted him with simple words and gestures. His parent says he hits his own tummy. You are about to examine his abdomen at the GP clinic. Which approach is most likely to pick up tenderness reliably?
options: Ask him to rate his pain 0 to 10 on a number scale as you press each quadrant
Let him keep his tablet, palpate gently starting away from the area and watch his face
Start with deep palpation of the left iliac fossa to find the sore spot quickly
Ask his parent to hold his arms still so you can complete a full abdominal exam
questions.why: In a non-verbal child, pain is judged from behaviour: grimacing, guarding and a rise in heart rate. Keeping him calm with a familiar object and palpating gently, starting away from the suspected area, lets you see these signs before distress hides them.
notes: A numeric rating scale needs language and number concepts that Liam does not have, so his answers would not be reliable.
Starting deep at the likely painful spot will upset him, and then you cannot tell tenderness anywhere else from general distress.
Holding him down is distressing and makes guarding hard to interpret. Calm engagement got his cooperation in this station.

questions.stem: Liam, 10, 31 kg, passes hard pellet stools every 4 to 5 days and has soiled twice this week. He has a firm, tender left iliac fossa mass. He is afebrile, not vomiting and his abdomen is not distended. You are his GP. Which is the most appropriate first treatment for his faecal loading?
options: Oral macrogol, increasing the daily sachets until stools are soft and runny
Sodium phosphate enema in the clinic today, then advice on dietary fibre
Increase dietary fibre and fluids alone, and review him in 4 weeks
Lactulose 10 mL twice daily on its own until the stools soften
questions.why: For a child with faecal impaction, first-line treatment is oral macrogol disimpaction, with the dose increased step by step (RCH guideline) until the stools are soft and runny. Maintenance then continues for months, along with fluids, fibre and a toileting routine.
notes: Australian paediatric guidelines advise against enemas as first-line treatment in children. They are invasive and distressing, and phosphate enemas risk electrolyte problems, especially in a child who cannot cooperate.
Fibre and fluids support maintenance but cannot clear an established faecal mass. Waiting 4 weeks leaves him in pain.
Lactulose on its own is less effective than macrogol for disimpaction and often causes bloating and cramps.

questions.stem: Liam, 10, had his risperidone increased to 0.5 mg twice a day 6 weeks ago. Since then his parent says he is stiffer, drools more and cannot sit still. On examination at the GP clinic he has mild cogwheel rigidity and a tremor. Which mechanism best explains these findings?
options: Dopamine D2 receptor blockade in the mesolimbic pathway
Dopamine D2 receptor blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway
Dopamine D2 receptor blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway
Serotonin 5-HT2A receptor blockade in the cerebral cortex
questions.why: Blocking D2 receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway upsets the dopamine and acetylcholine balance in the basal ganglia. This causes extrapyramidal effects: parkinsonism (rigidity, tremor, drooling) and akathisia. Akathisia can look like agitation and lead to the dose being wrongly increased.
notes: Mesolimbic D2 blockade produces the intended antipsychotic and anti-aggression effect, not rigidity or tremor.
Tuberoinfundibular D2 blockade raises prolactin, which risperidone often does, but it does not cause movement disorders.
5-HT2A antagonism actually lowers the risk of extrapyramidal effects with atypical antipsychotics. It does not cause them.

questions.stem: Liam, 10, is non-verbal. He has been pulling at the left side of his face and refusing crunchy food. At the GP clinic you find a carious, tender lower left molar with swelling of the gum next to it. Which nerve carries pain from the pulp of this tooth?
options: Posterior superior alveolar nerve, from the maxillary division
Buccal branch of the facial nerve
Lingual nerve, from the mandibular division
Inferior alveolar nerve, from the mandibular division
questions.why: The mandibular teeth get their sensory supply from the inferior alveolar nerve, a branch of the mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve. It runs through the mandibular canal. Because V3 also supplies the ear and temple, dental pain can be referred there, which fits Liam pulling at his face.
notes: The posterior superior alveolar nerve (V2) supplies the upper molars, not the lower teeth.
The facial nerve's buccal branch is motor to the muscles of facial expression. It carries no sensation from the teeth.
The lingual nerve carries general sensation from the front two-thirds of the tongue and the lingual gum, not from the tooth pulp.
